summary.text: The Late Ordovician mass extinction, roughly 445 million years ago, is the first of the 'big five' mass extinctions in Earth's history.
It eliminated nearly 85% of marine species at a time when most complex multicellular life lived in the sea.
It is usually split into two pulses: one tied to a glaciation that cooled Earth and lowered sea levels, and one as the ice retreated amid widespread oxygen loss in the oceans.

facts.label: Size ranking
facts.value: Often called second-largest, behind the end-Permian

facts.label: Recovery time
facts.value: About the first 5 million years of the Silurian

items.prompt: A glaciation abruptly spreads over the continent of Gondwana, cooling the planet. Why would that harm animals living on shallow continental shelves?

options.label: Falling sea levels and cooling took away their habitat
Melting ice flooded the shelves with fresh water
The ice sheets slid into the sea and crushed them
Volcanoes beneath the ice poisoned the coastal water

items.explain: The glaciation brought cooling and a falling sea level, which caused habitat loss for many organisms along the continental shelves.

items.prompt: Two shellfish species share a shelf sea when the glaciation begins. Which one is more likely to vanish?

options.label: One that lives in waters at many different latitudes
One found only locally, coping with a narrow range of temperatures
One that can survive in both warm and cold water
One spread widely along coasts around the world

items.explain: Habitat loss hit endemic taxa with restricted temperature tolerance and latitudinal range especially hard.

items.prompt: During the cold spell, a cold-adapted group of brachiopods called the Hirnantia fauna spread into lower latitudes. What happened to it when the ice retreated?

options.label: It spread further and took over the warming seas
It moved onto land as the shelves dried out
It died out and was replaced by warm-water communities
It stayed unchanged throughout the following Silurian

items.explain: The Hirnantia fauna met its end in the second extinction pulse, replaced by Silurian-style assemblages adapted for warmer waters.

items.prompt: After the ice melted and warm conditions came back, a second wave of extinction struck. What was it linked to?

options.label: A large asteroid striking the ocean
A new advance of glaciers over the poles
Land plants spreading and crowding out sea life
Widespread loss of oxygen in the oceans

items.explain: The second pulse came as the glaciation receded and was associated with intense worldwide anoxia, or oxygen depletion, plus toxic sulfide production.

items.prompt: This event removed a huge share of sea species. How did it compare with other mass extinctions in reshaping how ecosystems were structured?

options.label: It changed ecosystem structure relatively little
It rebuilt ecosystems more than any other extinction
It wiped out all ocean ecosystems for millions of years
It moved most marine ecosystems onto dry land

items.explain: Despite its severity, it did not produce major changes to ecosystem structures compared to other mass extinctions, and had few of their long-term ecological impacts.

items.prompt: Two brachiopod species face the extinction. One is rare, the other is very common. Which had better odds of surviving?

options.label: The rare one, because it needs fewer resources
Both had equal odds, since abundance made no difference
The rare one, because predators overlook it
The common one, because abundance improved survival

items.explain: Brachiopods with higher abundance were more likely to survive the extinction.
